title: Jind Kaur's death, 1863
hook: she dies in London, and her son takes her ashes toward India

segments.voice: Yesterday, asees, and your line was she told him who he was. Did you ask an elder about where you come from? Today, that mother's last journey. Day nine hundred forty-four.

In a rented house in Kensington, with London's carriages passing in the street, a queen of the Punjab is dying. She has been a regent, a prisoner, a fugitive across the hills to Nepal, and, at the end, a mother living near her son. She will not see Lahore again. And when she dies, her son faces a question no English gentleman is trained for: how do you take your mother home? Today: Jind Kaur's death.
screen: `A RENTED HOUSE IN KENSINGTON.` → `A QUEEN WHO WON'T SEE LAHORE.` → `HOW DO YOU TAKE HER HOME?`

segments.voice: First, her last years. Jind Kaur lived in London near Duleep Singh after their meeting in Calcutta. Her health was poor and her sight was failing. But she kept telling him about the Punjab, and the histories suggest the stories took hold. Second, her death. She died in London, far from the land she had ruled as regent. Sikh custom is to cremate the body. In Victorian London that was not a simple thing to arrange, and her son wanted her rites done in India, not in England. Third, the journey. Duleep Singh took his mother's body by sea toward India. But he was not permitted to take her into the Punjab. So she was cremated on the banks of the Godavari river at Nasik, far to the south of the land she had known. A small memorial was built there. Her ashes, tradition says, were later moved to Lahore and laid near her husband's memorial, though that came long afterward. Fourth, how Sikh scripture speaks of death. In the Alahniyan, the songs of mourning by Guru Nanak in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that whoever has come must rise and go, and that this world is a passing show. At a Sikh funeral the hymns are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are given to flowing water. A son who had been raised far from all of it did what he could to carry his mother home, and got as close as he was allowed. That's today's line.
screen: `HER LAST YEARS IN LONDON.` · `A DEATH FAR FROM THE PUNJAB.` · `CREMATED BY THE GODAVARI.` · `WHOEVER COMES MUST GO.` · then, large: `ASHES CARRIED HOME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to remember a mother. Sit, and let your breath come and go. Bring to mind a mother: your own, someone else's, or a woman who mothered you without the name. Picture her hands doing something ordinary: stirring a pot, folding clothes, holding a cup. Stay with that picture. If she has died, let the memory rest in you without needing to do anything with it. If she's living, simply hold her in your mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Alahniyan, songs of mourning: Guru Nanak's say whoever has come must rise and go. The Maharani died in London, and her son carried her toward home. Today's word.
Your line: ashes carried home. Today, remember a mother, and say her name aloud once, to someone or to the empty room. Day nine hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: At a Sikh funeral, hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are placed in flowing water; Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur in histories and gatherings about the end of the kingdom.

notes: No year in the voice (the index title gives 1863). The hook's rain and carriages are scene-setting, not sourced.
Index hook says he took her ashes toward India; most accounts say he took her body and she was cremated at Nasik. Voice follows the latter; confirm and consider adjusting the index hook.
Later move of her ashes to Lahore (by her granddaughter Bamba Sutherland) given as 'tradition says' with no date; confirm.
Guru Nanak's Alahniyan (baabaa aaiaa hai uth chalanaa ih jag jhooth pasaaroaa) paraphrased; confirm Ang 579 and Gurmukhi ਭਾਣਾ.
